1. The animation shows a grid of tiles. Each tile appears to be one starting month, and the tile shows whether a buyer or a renter came out ahead from that start date. Light tiles mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark tiles mean the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation labels itself "illustrative", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. The pattern of dark tiles changes. In the first frames, the dark tiles form a band in the middle of the grid, with a few light tiles inside it. In later frames, a second dark strip appears at the left edge and the dark band shifts and widens. Most of the grid stays light. The "January 1991" label does not change across the frames. In the last two frames, a caption appears: "held five years: buyer ahead in 74.4%".

3. Across the historical periods shown, buying beat renting in most cases. The caption says that for a five-year hold, the buyer came out ahead in 74.4% of cases. The dark tiles are the periods when renting won, and they cluster in particular stretches of time. So the outcome depends on when you buy and how long you hold. Buying did not win every time, and the odds were not even.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer might take away that buying has usually paid off over holding periods of five to ten years, but that renting can win in some periods. The viewer might also take away that the result depends on timing and how long they stay.

5. The picture and on-screen text suggest the pattern: the light and dark tiles and the 74.4% caption. The advice in 4 is my own reading. The animation says only "history, not a forecast", which warns against treating the pattern as a prediction. It does not tell anyone to buy or rent.
